supports: Material grades, stainless steel specifications, dimensions

references.title: Vogel's Textbook of Quantitative Chemical Analysis (6th Edition)
supports: Solid reagent transfer techniques, balance weighing practices

name: Mortar and Pestle
purpose: Grinds, crushes, and pulverizes solid chemicals into fine, uniform powders.

image.alt: Heavy unglazed porcelain mortar bowl with pouring lip and rounded pestle club

description: A two-piece set consisting of a heavy, thick-walled bowl (mortar) with an unglazed interior and a baseball-bat shaped club (pestle) with a rounded unglazed grinding head. Crushes large crystals, granules, and biological tissues into fine powders through friction and compression.
commonUses: Grinding large chemical crystals into fine powders to accelerate dissolution rates
Homogenizing solid-solid mixtures for solid-state reactions and synthesis
Preparing potassium bromide (KBr) powder matrices for infrared pellet pressing
Crushing plant or biological tissues with sand or liquid nitrogen for biochemical extraction
types: Glazed porcelain mortar (exterior glazed, interior unglazed; classic chemistry workhorse)
Agate mortar and pestle (hard, non-porous microcrystalline quartz for analytical spectroscopy)
Glass mortar and pestle (smooth, non-porous, ideal for non-staining suspensions)
Alumina / Mullite mortar (extreme hardness and abrasion resistance)

capacity.notes: Standard student size has internal bowl volume of ~120 mL (outer diameter ~100 mm).

specifications.dimensions: Mortar outer diameter ~100 mm, Height ~60 mm; Pestle length ~115 mm, Head diameter ~30 mm

partsAndFunctions.function: Provides rough friction surface to grip and pulverize crystals during grinding
partsAndFunctions.handlingNotes: Avoid using metal spatulas that scratch or dislodge ceramic grit.

partsAndFunctions.function: Enables neat transfer of ground powder into paper or collection boats
partsAndFunctions.handlingNotes: Clean spout thoroughly before pouring.

partsAndFunctions.function: Matches the internal curvature radius of the mortar bowl to maximize grinding contact area
partsAndFunctions.handlingNotes: Grind with circular downward motion; do not hammer aggressively.

measurementAccuracy.notes: Not applicable: non-measuring mechanical comminution apparatus.

limitations: Porcelain is slightly porous and can absorb stains from intensely colored dyes or active organics
Must NEVER be used to grind explosive, friction-sensitive, or oxidizing mixtures (e.g. chlorates with sulfur)
Heavy and brittle; shatters if dropped on stone floors

preparation: Inspect mortar bowl and pestle head for cracks, chips, or residual colored powder
Confirm that the chemicals being ground are non-explosive and safe for mechanical friction
Place mortar on a non-slip rubber pad or bench mat to prevent sliding

steps.title: Loading Material
steps.instruction: Place coarse crystals into the mortar, filling to no more than one-third of the bowl depth.

steps.title: Coarse Crushing
steps.instruction: Grasp the pestle firmly and press downward with a gentle rocking motion to crack large chunks into smaller grains. Do not pound like a hammer.

steps.title: Circular Grinding
steps.instruction: Rotate the pestle head in firm, steady circular motions against the bowl walls and base, working outward from center to edge.

steps.title: Powder Collection
steps.instruction: Use a clean plastic or porcelain spatula to scrape powder from the pestle head and mortar walls toward the pouring spout, then pour into a weighing boat.

handlingTips: Never hammer or strike the pestle forcefully downward; use smooth circular grinding and crushing pressure
Place a piece of filter paper or weighing boat under the spout to catch powder when transferring
shutdown: Scrape out all usable ground powder
Wash mortar and pestle thoroughly with warm water and detergent, scrub with a stiff brush, and rinse with DI water
Dry thoroughly in an oven or air dry before storage

requiredPPE: Dust mask (essential when grinding fine or toxic powders)
hazards: Explosive detonation from friction-sensitive chemical mixtures
warnings: NEVER grind strong oxidizers (chlorates, perchlorates, nitrates) together with combustible materials (sulfur, carbon, organics); violent explosion hazard
Never hammer or pound the pestle forcefully against the mortar base
actionsToAvoid: Do not fill mortar more than one-third full (causes powder to spill over rim)
Do not grind toxic heavy metal salts without operating inside a certified fume hood
emergencyGuidance: If fine dust causes coughing or respiratory irritation, evacuate to fresh air immediately
In case of friction spark or fire, cover immediately with sand or use Class ABC extinguisher

cleaningSteps: Wash with warm water and scouring powder or laboratory detergent using a stiff nylon brush
For stubborn chemical stains, grind a small portion of clean white silica sand or potassium chloride to scour out the pores
Rinse four times with tap water, finish with deionized water, and dry in an oven up to 100 °C
storageInstructions: Store mortar with pestle resting inside it on low, sturdy shelves
Place a piece of clean cloth or tissue between pestle and mortar to prevent ceramic abrasion
maintenanceChecks: Inspect mortar bowl for hairline cracks under bright light
Inspect pestle head for ceramic chipping or uneven flat spots

troubleshooting.problem: Mortar is permanently stained by previous colored chemical
possibleCauses: Chemical dye or metal complex soaked into unglazed ceramic pores
solution: Grind a tablespoon of clean dry quartz sand or table salt in the mortar to physically scour the stained surface, then wash
prevention: Use an agate or glass mortar for strongly staining dyes and indicators

troubleshooting.problem: Powder dust flies out of the mortar during grinding
possibleCauses: Grinding too fast or vigorously; filled bowl beyond one-third capacity
solution: Slow down grinding motion; cover mortar opening with a clean filter paper perforated for the pestle shaft
prevention: Fill only to one-quarter capacity and grind gently

troubleshooting.problem: Pestle head chips, leaving ceramic fragments in the powder
possibleCauses: Pounded pestle downward like a hammer instead of grinding smoothly
solution: Discard contaminated powder batch; inspect pestle and retire if chipped
prevention: Always use firm circular rolling motions, never hammering impacts

commonMistakes.mistake: Pounding the pestle vertically like a hammer onto large crystals
commonMistakes.whyItMatters: Easily fractures the ceramic mortar bowl, sends crystal projectiles into eyes, and chips the pestle head
commonMistakes.howToAvoid: Apply steady downward crushing pressure with a gentle rocking motion, followed by circular grinding

commonMistakes.mistake: Grinding an oxidizer and a fuel together in a mortar
commonMistakes.whyItMatters: Friction and localized heat will cause spontaneous catastrophic explosion and severe trauma
commonMistakes.howToAvoid: Never grind oxidizers with fuels; grind reagents separately and mix gently by tumbling on paper

relatedEquipment.reason: Spatulas are used to scrape ground powder out of the mortar into collection vessels.
relatedEquipment.difference: The mortar and pestle performs mechanical comminution; the spatula transfers the powder.

relatedEquipment.reason: Ground powders are poured through the mortar spout into weighing boats for mass measurement.
relatedEquipment.difference: The mortar is the crushing tool; the weighing boat is the balance receptacle.

relatedEquipment.reason: Ground powders are transferred to beakers where their increased surface area accelerates dissolution.
relatedEquipment.difference: The mortar grinds dry solids; the beaker dissolves solids in liquids.

references.title: Vogel's Textbook of Practical Organic Chemistry (5th Edition)
Prudent Practices in the Laboratory (National Research Council)
supports: Explosive friction hazards, dust inhalation controls

name: Weighing Boat
purpose: Holds dry chemical solids and powders during mass measurement on laboratory balances.

image.alt: Square white polystyrene disposable weighing boat with sloping sides and pour-spout corners

description: A shallow, flexible disposable dish made of polystyrene or aluminum with a flat bottom and sloping sides. Designed to sit stably on balance pans to contain solids during weighing, featuring flexible corners that squeeze together to form a pouring spout for clean, spill-free transfer.
commonUses: Containing solid chemical reagents while weighing on analytical and top-pan balances
Transferring weighed powders cleanly into volumetric flasks and beakers by squeezing corners
Holding small liquid or moisture samples for drying and moisture analysis (aluminum boats)
Temporary bench tray for sorting small magnetic stir bars, stoppers, and test items
types: Polystyrene standard square/diamond weigh boat (flexible, biologically inert, smooth non-stick surface)
Antistatic weighing boat (treated to reduce static charge repulsion of fine fluffy powders)
Aluminum weighing dish (heat-resistant for moisture balance drying ovens and organic solvents)

capacity.notes: Small (~20 mL), Medium (~100 mL), Large (~250 mL); holds solid masses from 0.01 g up to 200 g.

specifications.dimensions: Small: ~45 × 45 mm, Medium: ~80 × 80 mm, Height ~20 mm

partsAndFunctions.function: Rests flat and stably on the circular balance pan without rocking
partsAndFunctions.handlingNotes: Keep bottom clean and dry before placing on balance.

partsAndFunctions.function: Contain powders securely while allowing easy spatula access
partsAndFunctions.handlingNotes: Do not overload past sidewall rim.

partsAndFunctions.function: Flex inward when squeezed to create a funnel spout for neat powder transfer
partsAndFunctions.handlingNotes: Squeeze opposite sides gently to pour.

measurementAccuracy.notes: Not applicable: consumable sample receptacle; balance provides all measurement accuracy.

limitations: Polystyrene boats dissolve and melt if exposed to organic solvents (acetone, dichloromethane, toluene)
Static electricity can cause very fine powders to scatter or cling to walls
Cannot be heated in drying ovens above 80 °C (polystyrene deforms; use aluminum instead)

preparation: Select appropriate size matching the quantity of chemical being weighed
Inspect boat to ensure it is clean, dry, and dust-free
Open the balance draft door and place the boat centrally on the balance pan

steps.title: Taring the Balance
steps.instruction: Close balance draft doors and press the TARE (or ZERO) button so the balance displays exactly 0.0000 g.

steps.title: Adding Chemical
steps.instruction: Using a clean spatula, transfer the solid reagent into the center of the boat until the target mass is reached.

steps.title: Mass Recording
steps.instruction: Close the draft doors, allow the balance stability indicator to illuminate, and record the final mass in your notebook.

steps.title: Dispensing
steps.instruction: Carefully remove the boat from the balance pan. Squeeze opposite sides to flex a corner into a pouring funnel, and tip the powder smoothly into the target vessel.

handlingTips: Squeeze two diagonal or opposite corners together to form an instant funnel for pouring directly into narrow flask necks
Tap the back of the boat lightly with a spatula to dislodge clinging particles into the target vessel
shutdown: Dispose of single-use plastic weighing boats in the solid laboratory waste container
Wipe balance pan with a soft brush if any powder grains spilled outside the boat
Close balance draft shield doors

hazards: Spill on balance pan corroding load cell
warnings: Never add chemicals to a weighing boat while it is resting on the balance pan if handling corrosive fuming reagents (weigh outside, or dispense carefully)
Never put acetone or volatile solvents into polystyrene weighing boats
actionsToAvoid: Do not blow with your breath on the balance pan to clear spilled powder (inhales dust and alters calibration)
Do not reuse disposable plastic boats across different chemical reagents
emergencyGuidance: If toxic chemical powder spills onto the balance or bench, sweep immediately with balance brush into waste
In case of skin contact, wash thoroughly with soap and water

cleaningSteps: Weighing boats are designed primarily as single-use disposable consumables
If reusing for non-critical salt weighing, rinse with deionized water and dry with clean lint-free paper
Discard if stained, scratched, or distorted
storageInstructions: Store nested in original dispenser boxes to prevent airborne dust accumulation
Store in a dry location away from heat and direct sunlight
maintenanceChecks: Check that stored boats remain clean and free from environmental dust
Verify antistatic coating effectiveness if handling fine powders

troubleshooting.problem: Balance reading drifts or jumps erratically when boat is placed on pan
possibleCauses: Static electricity charge on the polystyrene boat repelling balance frame
solution: Use an antistatic weighing boat, an antistatic ionizer strip, or switch to an aluminum boat
prevention: Avoid rubbing plastic boats against synthetic clothing or latex gloves

troubleshooting.problem: Weighing boat softens, dissolves, or becomes sticky
possibleCauses: Added an organic solvent (acetone, ester, aromatic hydrocarbon) into polystyrene
solution: Discard immediately into solvent waste; use glass weighing bottles or aluminum boats for organic liquids
prevention: Never use polystyrene with non-aqueous solvents

troubleshooting.problem: Powder clings to the plastic boat and will not pour into flask
possibleCauses: Electrostatic attraction on dry winter days; fine crystal particle size
solution: Rinse residual powder from the boat into the receiver using a wash bottle of solvent, or use antistatic boats
prevention: Use antistatic boats or weigh by difference using glass weighing bottles

commonMistakes.mistake: Adding chemical crystals directly from a bottle without using a weighing boat
commonMistakes.whyItMatters: Chemicals spill onto the metal balance pan, corroding the balance mechanism and ruining calibration
commonMistakes.howToAvoid: Always place a weighing boat or container on the pan and tare before dispensing chemicals

commonMistakes.mistake: Blowing with your mouth to clear spilled powder off the balance pan
commonMistakes.whyItMatters: Blows toxic chemical aerosols directly into your eyes and face and forces powder into delicate balance electronics
commonMistakes.howToAvoid: Use a soft camel-hair balance brush to sweep powder onto a piece of paper for disposal

relatedEquipment.reason: Weighing boats sit directly on the analytical balance pan to contain chemicals during weighing.
relatedEquipment.difference: The balance measures the mass; the boat holds the chemical.

relatedEquipment.reason: Spatulas transfer chemical powders from reagent bottles into weighing boats.
relatedEquipment.difference: The spatula is the transfer tool; the boat is the holding dish.

relatedEquipment.reason: Powder weighed in the boat is funneled into the volumetric flask to prepare standard solutions.
relatedEquipment.difference: The weighing boat holds dry solid; the volumetric flask dissolves and measures total liquid volume.

references.title: ASTM E319 - Standard Practice for the Evaluation of Single-Pan Mechanical Balances
Vogel's Textbook of Quantitative Chemical Analysis (6th Edition)

name: Filter Paper
purpose: Separates suspended insoluble solid particles from liquids during gravity or vacuum filtration.

image.alt: Circular white cellulose filter paper disc folded in quarters and seated in a funnel

description: A semi-permeable circular sheet composed of cellulose fibers or glass microfibers arranged randomly. Acts as a physical barrier that permits fluid permeation while retaining solid particulate matter, essential for gravimetric analysis and chemical separation.
commonUses: Separating precipitates from supernatants during gravity filtration in a glass funnel
Retaining crystal crops during vacuum filtration inside a Büchner funnel
Gravimetric quantitative analysis using ashless filter paper ignited in crucibles
Clarifying cloudy reaction solutions and removing drying agents (e.g. MgSO4)
types: Qualitative filter paper (standard student lab grade, e.g. Whatman Grade 1, ~11 µm pore size)
Quantitative ashless filter paper (acid-washed, burns away leaving <0.01% ash for gravimetric weighing)
Glass microfiber filter paper (fast flow rate, high chemical and heat resistance up to 500 °C)

capacity.notes: Diameter ranges from 42.5 mm to 240 mm (110 mm and 125 mm are standard laboratory sizes).

specifications.dimensions: Thickness ~0.18 mm, Typical particle retention ~11 µm (Whatman Grade 1 standard)

partsAndFunctions.function: Traps solid particles on the surface (cake filtration) and within fiber interstices (depth filtration)
partsAndFunctions.handlingNotes: Avoid tearing during folding.

partsAndFunctions.function: Permits liquid solvent molecules to pass freely under gravity or vacuum while stopping particles
partsAndFunctions.handlingNotes: Select pore size rating matching precipitate grain size.

partsAndFunctions.function: Forms the top boundary of the filtration cone; must remain lower than funnel rim
partsAndFunctions.handlingNotes: Trim if paper exceeds funnel height.

measurementAccuracy.notes: Not applicable: porous separation consumable; nominal pore size defines particle retention cutoff (e.g. 11 µm).

limitations: Degraded and weakened by concentrated acids, hot alkalis, and strong oxidizing reagents
Gelatinous precipitates (e.g., iron hydroxide) rapidly blind and clog cellulose pores
Cannot be weighed accurately for quantitative mass without drying to constant weight (hygroscopic)

preparation: Choose correct grade and diameter (paper circle when folded must fit 1 cm below funnel rim)
Ensure funnel is clean and mounted securely on a support ring or flask
Have solvent wash bottle ready for wetting the paper

steps.title: Folding in Quarters
steps.instruction: Fold circular filter paper disc in half, then fold in half again to form a quarter-circle. Tear off a tiny corner from the outside fold to improve the seal.

steps.title: Cone Opening
steps.instruction: Open the quarter-circle into a cone (three thicknesses on one side, one thickness on the other).

steps.title: Seating and Wetting
steps.instruction: Place cone into the glass funnel and wet lightly with a squirt of solvent (e.g. distilled water). Press edges gently against glass to form an airtight seal.

steps.title: Filtration
steps.instruction: Pour suspension into the center of the cone using a glass stirring rod. Always keep the liquid level at least 5 mm below the top edge of the paper.

handlingTips: Tearing a small corner off the outer fold before opening into a cone helps establish a tighter vacuum seal along the funnel glass wall
For faster gravity filtration, use fluted (pleated) filter paper to increase effective surface area
shutdown: Allow all liquid to drain completely through the paper
Carefully lift filter paper containing precipitate with forceps or a spatula
Dispose of spent filter paper in designated solid waste or transfer to an oven/desiccator for drying

hazards: Chemical exposure from tearing during filtration
warnings: Do not filter concentrated nitric or sulfuric acid through standard cellulose paper (paper oxidizes/chars)
Never allow liquid to rise above the top edge of the filter paper
actionsToAvoid: Do not poke stirring rods into the apex of the paper cone (punctures paper instantly)
Do not apply high vacuum to standard thin cellulose filter paper without a support mesh
emergencyGuidance: If filter paper tears and hazardous chemicals spill below, isolate the receiver and re-filter using a fresh paper
Treat skin contact with filtrate by washing under running water for 15 minutes

cleaningSteps: Filter paper is a single-use consumable and is never washed or reused
Dispose of spent paper and trapped residues according to chemical waste guidelines
storageInstructions: Store in original packaging boxes in a clean, dry cabinet to protect from moisture, dust, and laboratory acid fumes
Keep away from open chemical reagent shelves
maintenanceChecks: Inspect filter paper discs before use for tears, creases, or discoloration
Verify correct grade (qualitative vs quantitative ashless) before critical gravimetric assays

troubleshooting.problem: Liquid drains extremely slowly through the filter paper
possibleCauses: Precipitate particles are fine or gelatinous and plugged the pores
Unfluted smooth paper used
solution: Flute (pleat) the filter paper before seating, or switch to a coarser pore grade or vacuum filtration
prevention: Allow precipitate to digest (grow larger crystals) in warm solution before filtering

troubleshooting.problem: Filtrate passes through cloudy instead of crystal clear
possibleCauses: Paper pore size is larger than precipitate particle diameter
Liquid spilled over paper rim
Paper cone torn at apex
solution: Switch to a finer retention grade (e.g., Whatman Grade 5 or 42) and re-filter cloudy liquid
prevention: Match paper pore rating to precipitate; never pour over the top paper rim

troubleshooting.problem: Paper tears at the apex when liquid is poured in
possibleCauses: Poked with a glass stirring rod
Poured heavy liquid stream directly into the point
solution: Discard torn paper and re-filter mixture through a new, properly seated filter paper cone
prevention: Direct the stream against the side of the cone using a glass rod, never dropping onto the tip

commonMistakes.mistake: Filling the liquid mixture past the top rim of the filter paper
commonMistakes.whyItMatters: Unfiltered suspension flows over the edge and behind the paper directly into the stem, ruining the filtration
commonMistakes.howToAvoid: Always maintain liquid level at least 5 mm below the top edge of the filter paper cone

commonMistakes.mistake: Poking the tip of a glass stirring rod into the bottom apex of the paper cone
commonMistakes.whyItMatters: Instantly punches a hole through the wet, fragile cellulose, dumping all precipitate into the filtrate
commonMistakes.howToAvoid: Keep the glass stirring rod hovering above the paper and pour down the rod gently

relatedEquipment.reason: Filter paper is folded and seated inside the glass funnel to perform gravity filtration.
relatedEquipment.difference: The glass funnel provides the rigid cone support; the filter paper is the porous filtration medium.

relatedEquipment.reason: Flat filter paper discs are placed flat over the perforated plate in Büchner vacuum filtration.
relatedEquipment.difference: The Büchner funnel is the vacuum filtration funnel; the filter paper is the retention filter.

relatedEquipment.reason: Beakers collect the clarified filtrate draining through the filter paper.
relatedEquipment.difference: The filter paper performs the separation; the beaker collects and contains the filtrate.

references.title: ASTM E832 - Standard Specification for Laboratory Filter Papers
supports: Pore retention grades, flow rates, wet burst strength

references.title: Vogel's Textbook of Quantitative Chemical Analysis (6th Edition)
supports: Paper folding methods, gravimetric ashless filtration

name: Evaporating Dish
purpose: Evaporates excess solvents to concentrate solutions or recover dry crystalline solutes under direct heat.

image.alt: Shallow glazed porcelain evaporating dish with pouring spout and wide liquid surface

description: A shallow, wide-mouthed porcelain or borosilicate ceramic dish with a pouring spout. Designed with a high surface-area-to-depth ratio to maximize solvent evaporation rates, capable of withstanding direct flame heating and high temperatures up to several hundred degrees Celsius.
commonUses: Evaporating aqueous solvent to dryness to isolate inorganic salts
Concentrating dilute solutions prior to fractional crystallization
Drying moist solid precipitates over a steam or sand bath
Testing for total dissolved solids (TDS) in water quality testing

steps.title: Filling
steps.instruction: Pour the solution into the evaporating dish, filling to no more than one-half to two-thirds capacity to prevent boiling over.

steps.title: Heating
steps.instruction: Heat gently with a Bunsen burner flame through a wire gauze, or place over a boiling water bath for gentle indirect heating.

steps.title: Monitoring Concentration
steps.instruction: As solvent volume decreases, reduce burner flame intensity. Stir gently with a glass rod to prevent crystal crust formation.

steps.title: Drying and Cooling
steps.instruction: Turn off flame before the liquid is completely gone; use residual dish heat to finish drying. Transfer dish using crucible tongs to a heat-resistant tile or desiccator.

handlingTips: Use crucible tongs or heat-resistant gloves to handle evaporating dishes; never touch bare-handed
Turn off heat when only a small film of liquid remains; latent heat will evaporate the rest without spattering crystals
shutdown: Allow dish to cool completely to room temperature before washing
Scrape out recovered dry crystal product using a spatula
Wash with detergent and water, rinse with DI water, and dry

hazards: Severe thermal burns from hot porcelain
warnings: Never peer directly down into an evaporating dish while heating; hot liquid and crystals can spatter violently
Do not place a hot evaporating dish onto a cold, wet countertop (thermal shock will shatter it)
actionsToAvoid: Do not pick up a hot evaporating dish with bare fingers or thin nitrile gloves
Do not evaporate flammable organic solvents over an open burner flame
emergencyGuidance: If hot solution spatters into eyes, flush immediately at eyewash station for 15 minutes
Treat contact burns by holding under cool running water for at least 10 minutes

cleaningSteps: Let dish cool completely to room temperature
Soak in warm water and scrub with laboratory detergent and a sponge
For baked-on mineral residues, soak with dilute 1 M hydrochloric acid, then rinse four times with tap water and once with DI water
storageInstructions: Store stacked in organized drawers or cupboards, separated by size
Place paper towels between dishes to prevent glaze scratching
maintenanceChecks: Inspect glaze under strong light for fine network cracks (crazing)
Tap gently with a wooden pencil; a clear ring indicates sound ceramic, a dull thud indicates a hidden crack

troubleshooting.problem: Crystals violently spatter and pop out of the dish as dryness approaches
possibleCauses: Heated too strongly near dryness; steam trapped under crystal crust expands explosively
solution: Turn off flame early and finish evaporation over a gentle steam bath or with residual heat
prevention: Reduce heat significantly once crystals begin forming on liquid surface

troubleshooting.problem: Porcelain dish cracks during heating
possibleCauses: Applied intense flame to wet base
Pre-existing hairline fracture in ceramic
solution: Extinguish flame immediately, allow to cool, and treat contents as waste
prevention: Always ensure outer base is dry and use a wire gauze to diffuse heat

troubleshooting.problem: Stained residue cannot be removed with detergent
possibleCauses: Metal oxide or salt baked into ceramic micro-pores
solution: Soak in warm dilute nitric or hydrochloric acid for 30 minutes, then scrub with scouring pad
prevention: Do not overheat salts beyond their decomposition temperature

commonMistakes.mistake: Looking directly down into the evaporating dish while heating strongly
commonMistakes.whyItMatters: Decrepitating salt crystals pop out like hot shrapnel, striking eyes and face
commonMistakes.howToAvoid: View from an angle from behind safety goggles or place a watch glass loosely over the dish with a gap

commonMistakes.mistake: Setting a red-hot porcelain dish directly onto a cold laminated bench
commonMistakes.whyItMatters: The sudden thermal shock cracks the dish in half and scorches the benchtop
commonMistakes.howToAvoid: Always place hot porcelain dishes onto a ceramic-centered wire gauze or heat-resistant ceramic tile
